title: Euenius · lines 65–72
subtitle: Not knowing of the oracle, Euenius asks for the finest land and the finest house, and is held to his word

units.en: Not having heard the oracle, he made his choice, saying that if he were given certain fields, the finest in Apollonia, and on top of that the house he knew was the finest in the town,

notes.label: Dramatic irony
notes.body: The reader knows the gods have promised him whatever he asks, but Euenius does not, so every word of his request is read with that in mind.

notes.label: Superlative
notes.body: He asks for the very best land and the very best house, which shows he is aiming high.

notes.label: Parallelism
notes.quote: κάλλιστοι ὄντες τῶν ἐν τῇ Ἀπολλωνίᾳ … καλλίστην οὖσαν τῶν ἐν πόλει
notes.trans: the finest in Apollonia … the finest in the town
notes.body: The two phrases are built the same way, so the land and the house make a neat matching pair.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: He adds a house to the land, so the reader sees his demand growing as he speaks.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Euenius knows exactly which house is the finest, which makes his request precise and personal.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: The word comes from μῆνις, the wrath of gods and heroes, which suggests how deep his anger has been.

notes.label: Parallelism
notes.trans: he would be without resentment … it would be enough
notes.body: Two matching clauses with ἄν close his request, so he offers to end the matter for good.

notes.label: Contrast (μέν ... δέ)
notes.body: Euenius speaks and the citizens answer at once, so the reader feels the trap snap shut.

notes.label: Fast pace
notes.body: They reply the moment he finishes, which gives him no time to change his mind.

notes.label: Direct speech
notes.body: The reveal is given in the citizens' own words, so the reader hears exactly what Euenius hears.

notes.label: Repetition
notes.body: The citizens pick up Euenius' own word at once, which shows they are holding him to it.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The object comes first in their reply, so the stress falls on the payment he has just agreed to.

notes.label: Irony
notes.body: They claim to be paying in full, yet they are paying only what a tricked man asked for.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The oracles are mentioned last, so the twist comes at the very end of the sentence, just as it hits Euenius.

questions: Was Euenius' request modest or greedy? Think about what else he might have asked for.
How does the word order of lines 70–72 make the citizens' reply so effective?
